0.title: Jonah: Salvation Belongs to the LORD

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Now the word of the LORD came to Jonah the son of Amittai, saying,<sup>2</sup>"Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before me."<sup>3</sup>But Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD. He went down to Joppa and found a ship going to Tarshish. So he paid the fare and went down into it, to go with them to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD.<sup>4</sup>But the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea, and there was a mighty tempest on the sea, so that the ship threatened to break up.<sup>5</sup>Then the mariners were afraid, and each cried out to his god. And they hurled the cargo that was in the ship into the sea to lighten it for them. But Jonah had gone down into the inner part of the ship and had lain down and was fast asleep.<sup>6</sup>So the captain came and said to him, "What do you mean, you sleeper? Arise, call out to your god! Perhaps the god will give a thought to us, that we may not perish."<sup>7</sup>And they said to one another, "Come, let us cast lots, that we may know on whose account this evil has come upon us." So they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah.<sup>8</sup>Then they said to him, "Tell us on whose account this evil has come upon us. What is your occupation? And where do you come from? What is your country? And of what people are you?"<sup>9</sup>And he said to them, "I am a Hebrew, and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land."<sup>10</sup>Then the men were exceedingly afraid and said to him, "What is this that you have done!" For the men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the LORD, because he had told them.<sup>11</sup>Then they said to him, "What shall we do to you, that the sea may quiet down for us?" For the sea grew more and more tempestuous.<sup>12</sup>He said to them, "Pick me up and hurl me into the sea; then the sea will quiet down for you, for I know it is because of me that this great tempest has come upon you."<sup>13</sup>Nevertheless, the men rowed hard to get back to dry land, but they could not, for the sea grew more and more tempestuous against them.<sup>14</sup>Therefore they called out to the LORD, "O LORD, let us not perish for this man's life, and lay not on us innocent blood, for you, O LORD, have done as it pleased you."<sup>15</sup>So they picked up Jonah and hurled him into the sea, and the sea ceased from its raging.<sup>16</sup>Then the men feared the LORD exceedingly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows.<sup>17</sup>And the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Call and the Flight
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God tells Jonah, Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it (vv. 1-2). Instead, Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, going down to Joppa, paying the fare and going down into a ship (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: God sends his word to a city that deserves judgment, and his own prophet runs the other way.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the word of the LORD came to Jonah the son of Amittai, saying, "Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before me." But Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD. He went down to Joppa and found a ship going to Tarshish. So he paid the fare and went down into it, to go with them to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the word of the LORD came to Jonah the son of Amittai, saying,

Jonah was a real prophet in Israel's history. The book of Kings tells us that Jonah the son of Amittai, the prophet, who was from Gath-hepher announced that King Jeroboam II would restore Israel's borders (2 Kgs 14:25). Gath-hepher was a village in the north, in Galilee. So Jonah preached in the eighth century BC, in the same years as Amos and Hosea, when Israel was prosperous and Assyria was rising in the east.

That earlier message had been good news for Israel: expanded borders, national success. This message is different, and Jonah will hate it.

Some Christians read this book as a parable rather than a record of events, because of the fish and the sudden repentance of a whole city. Most in the Reformed tradition take it as history, chiefly because Jesus did. He spoke of Jonah in the belly of the fish and of the men of Nineveh who repented at the preaching of Jonah as real people and real events, and compared them to his own death and resurrection (Matt 12:39-41). These notes read it the same way. Either way, the book's message is the same, and it is aimed squarely at the reader.

"Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before me."

Nineveh was a great city of Assyria, founded long before (Gen 10:11-12) and later the capital of the empire. The Assyrians were the terror of the ancient world, famous for cruelty to the peoples they conquered. Nahum would later call Nineveh the bloody city, all full of lies and plunder (Nah 3:1). They were also the nation that would eventually destroy Jonah's own country (2 Kgs 17:6). Asking an Israelite to preach there was like asking someone to carry a warning to the headquarters of an enemy army that had burned his neighbours' villages.

Their evil has come up before me. (The ESV notes that this Hebrew word can mean either "evil" or "disaster", and it runs right through the book.) God has seen it. That is important: the message to Nineveh is not a pleasant one. Jonah is sent to announce judgment.

But Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD. He went down to Joppa and found a ship going to Tarshish. So he paid the fare and went down into it, to go with them to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD.

God said Arise, go; Jonah rose to flee. Nineveh lay hundreds of miles to the east, overland. Tarshish lay far to the west across the Mediterranean, probably in Spain: as far in the opposite direction as a man could buy a ticket. He went down to Joppa, the port, and went down into the ship. Watch that word. Jonah goes down to Joppa, down into the ship, down into the inner part of it (v. 5), down into the sea, and down to the roots of the mountains (2:6). Sin always has a downward staircase, and every step feels like a decision we are making freely. He even paid the fare. Running from God is never free.

What does it mean to flee from the presence of the LORD? Jonah was a prophet; he knew that God fills heaven and earth, and he says so himself in verse 9. He was not trying to find a place outside God's reach. He was resigning. He was walking out of God's service and away from the land where God had placed him. People still do this. We cannot escape God's presence, as the psalm says: If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me (Ps 139:9-10). But we can stop praying, stop meeting with God's people, and put distance between ourselves and the thing God has told us to do.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea, and the sailors cry each to his own god while Jonah sleeps below (vv. 4-5). The captain wakes him: Arise, call out to your god! (v. 6). The lot falls on Jonah, who answers, I am a Hebrew, and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land (vv. 7-9). The sailors are appalled: What is this that you have done! (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: There is no running from God, and a believer's disobedience puts others in the storm with him.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea, and there was a mighty tempest on the sea, so that the ship threatened to break up. Then the mariners were afraid, and each cried out to his god. And they hurled the cargo that was in the ship into the sea to lighten it for them. But Jonah had gone down into the inner part of the ship and had lain down and was fast asleep. So the captain came and said to him, "What do you mean, you sleeper? Arise, call out to your god! Perhaps the god will give a thought to us, that we may not perish."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea, and there was a mighty tempest on the sea, so that the ship threatened to break up.

The first But was Jonah's (v. 3). This But is God's, and it settles the matter. God hurled a great wind, as a man hurls a spear. The storm is not bad luck; it is the pursuit of a runaway prophet by the God who will not let him go. Say it plainly: this storm is mercy. God could have let Jonah sail away.

Then the mariners were afraid, and each cried out to his god. And they hurled the cargo that was in the ship into the sea to lighten it for them. But Jonah had gone down into the inner part of the ship and had lain down and was fast asleep.

These were experienced sailors, and they were terrified, which tells us how bad the storm was. They did two sensible things: they prayed, each to his god, and they hurled the cargo overboard, sacrificing their profit to save their lives.

Meanwhile the one man on board who knew the true God was asleep. The contrast is deliberate and damning. Pagans pray while the prophet sleeps through a crisis he caused. Spiritual sleep is like that: the further we run from God, the less we feel the danger.

Christians cannot read this without thinking of another boat in another storm, where Jesus lay asleep on the cushion while his disciples panicked (Mark 4:38). But the two sleepers are opposites. Jonah slept in rebellion, and the storm was his fault; Jesus slept in perfect peace, and then rebuked the wind so that there was a great calm (Mark 4:39). Jonah must be thrown into the sea to save the crew; Jesus speaks and saves them all. As the disciples asked, Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him? (Mark 4:41).

So the captain came and said to him, "What do you mean, you sleeper? Arise, call out to your god! Perhaps the god will give a thought to us, that we may not perish."

Now the captain of a pagan crew has to tell a prophet of God to pray. Notice his words: Arise, call out. They are the very words God used in verse 2, Arise, go ... and call out. God's command catches up with Jonah in the mouth of an unbeliever. It is a humbling thing when someone outside the faith shames a Christian into doing what God had already commanded.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to one another, "Come, let us cast lots, that we may know on whose account this evil has come upon us." So they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah. Then they said to him, "Tell us on whose account this evil has come upon us. What is your occupation? And where do you come from? What is your country? And of what people are you?" And he said to them, "I am a Hebrew, and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land." Then the men were exceedingly afraid and said to him, "What is this that you have done!" For the men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the LORD, because he had told them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they said to one another, "Come, let us cast lots, that we may know on whose account this evil has come upon us." So they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah.

Casting lots was the ancient way of asking heaven a question. Normally it might mean nothing. This time God directs it exactly, as Proverbs says: The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD (Prov 16:33). There is nowhere left to hide. God has been closing in on Jonah through wind, waves and now a pebble in a sailor's hand.

Then they said to him, "Tell us on whose account this evil has come upon us. What is your occupation? And where do you come from? What is your country? And of what people are you?"

The questions come tumbling out. It is a strange kind of mercy that a man should be asked, in one breath, who he is and what he does, when both answers condemn him. What is your occupation? I am a prophet of God, running away from God.

And he said to them, "I am a Hebrew, and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land."

Jonah's answer is perfectly orthodox and painfully ironic. He says I fear the LORD while running from him. He confesses that God made the sea and the dry land, which are precisely the two places he has been trying to use as an escape route: the sea he is sailing on and the dry land he came from. You can hold a completely correct doctrine of God and live as if none of it were true. Before we shake our heads at Jonah, we should ask what we confess on Sunday and contradict on Monday.

Then the men were exceedingly afraid and said to him, "What is this that you have done!" For the men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the LORD, because he had told them.

The sailors are more shocked by Jonah's behaviour than he is. What is this that you have done! is not really a question; it is horror. They can see what a believer half-asleep in his sin cannot: that running from the Maker of sea and land is madness.

And notice the quiet detail at the end: because he had told them. Jonah had already explained, presumably over a meal, that he was running away from God. He had made his rebellion into conversation. Sin talked about casually is still sin, and the people around us usually understand that better than we do.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jonah tells them, Pick me up and hurl me into the sea (vv. 11-12). The sailors row hard to save him, then pray to the LORD and throw him overboard, and the sea ceased from its raging (vv. 13-15). The men feared the LORD exceedingly and offered sacrifice (v. 16). And the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow up Jonah (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: God saves pagan sailors through the sin of his prophet, and saves the prophet himself by a fish.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they said to him, "What shall we do to you, that the sea may quiet down for us?" For the sea grew more and more tempestuous. He said to them, "Pick me up and hurl me into the sea; then the sea will quiet down for you, for I know it is because of me that this great tempest has come upon you." Nevertheless, the men rowed hard to get back to dry land, but they could not, for the sea grew more and more tempestuous against them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they said to him, "What shall we do to you, that the sea may quiet down for us?" For the sea grew more and more tempestuous.

He said to them, "Pick me up and hurl me into the sea; then the sea will quiet down for you, for I know it is because of me that this great tempest has come upon you."

This is the first honest thing Jonah has done: it is because of me. He takes responsibility, and he offers his life to save the crew. Some read this as repentance and some as despair, a man who would rather drown than go to Nineveh. Both may be true at once. Even now he does not offer to pray for the storm to stop, or to turn the ship around and obey.

Yet God is doing something greater here than Jonah understands. One man is thrown into the deep so that many are saved, and the storm falls silent. Centuries later Caiaphas said, without knowing what he was saying, it is better for you that one man should die for the people (John 11:50). Jonah is a reluctant, half-hearted picture of the willing Saviour: Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God (1 Pet 3:18). The difference is that Jonah deserved the storm and Jesus did not.

Nevertheless, the men rowed hard to get back to dry land, but they could not, for the sea grew more and more tempestuous against them.

Look at these pagan sailors. Rather than throw a man overboard, they rowed hard (the ESV notes the Hebrew picture is that the men "dug in" their oars), risking their own lives to save the man who had endangered them. Remember this when we come to chapter 4. The sailors do everything they can to save one Hebrew; Jonah will be furious that God saves a city. The people we write off often show more compassion than we do.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore they called out to the LORD, "O LORD, let us not perish for this man's life, and lay not on us innocent blood, for you, O LORD, have done as it pleased you." So they picked up Jonah and hurled him into the sea, and the sea ceased from its raging. Then the men feared the LORD exceedingly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore they called out to the LORD, "O LORD, let us not perish for this man's life, and lay not on us innocent blood, for you, O LORD, have done as it pleased you."

Something remarkable has happened. In verse 5 each cried out to his god; now they call on the LORD, the covenant name of the God of Israel. They pray a careful prayer: do not hold us guilty of innocent blood, and they acknowledge that God have done as it pleased you, that he rules the storm and the sea. These sailors have learned more theology in one night than some learn in a lifetime.

So they picked up Jonah and hurled him into the sea, and the sea ceased from its raging.

The third hurl of the chapter. God hurled the wind, the sailors hurled the cargo, and now they hurl the prophet. The moment he hits the water, the sea is still. God's word does not fail; when the cause of the storm is dealt with, the storm is over.

Then the men feared the LORD exceedingly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows.

Here is the first conversion in the book, and it is pagan sailors, not Israelites. In verse 5 they were afraid of the storm; now they feared the LORD. They worship him with a sacrifice and commit themselves with vows. This is the pattern of real faith: reverence, worship, commitment.

And God did this through a disobedient prophet who never preached them a sermon. God is not limited by his servants' failures, though that is no excuse for failing. If the message of this book were "God loves Israel and judges the nations", the first chapter has already exploded it. Salvation is reaching foreigners in the middle of the sea while the prophet sinks.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.

(In the Hebrew Bible this verse begins chapter 2, as the ESV notes.) The word appointed is the key to the rest of the book. God appointed the fish here, and later he appoints a plant, a worm and a scorching wind (4:6-8). He is in command of the whole creation, great and small, and he uses all of it to deal with one stubborn man. (The ESV notes the verb may be read "had appointed", which would mean the fish was already on its way before Jonah hit the water.)

Scripture says a great fish, not a whale, and it does not tell us what kind. The point is not the biology; it is the sovereignty. The sea that Jonah used as an escape route has become God's instrument, and its creatures obey him. Amos said the same in his own way: even at the bottom of the sea God can reach a runaway (Amos 9:3).

Most importantly, this is where the swallowed prophet becomes a sign of Christ. Jesus said, just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth (Matt 12:40). Jonah went into the deep because of his own sin; Jesus went into death because of ours. Jonah was spat out on the shore; Jesus rose in glory. And Jesus added the words that should make every reader of this book tremble: something greater than Jonah is here (Matt 12:41).

Notice, finally, what the fish actually is. Jonah has just been thrown into the sea to drown, and God sends a fish. It looks like the end of him; it is his rescue. God's strangest providences are often his kindest. Many believers can look back at some dark swallowing time, the illness, the failure, the collapse, and say that it was the fish God sent to save them.

1.title: Fleeing from the Presence of the LORD
1.overview:
The word of the LORD comes to Jonah the son of Amittai: arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before God. Instead Jonah rises to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD, going down to Joppa, paying the fare and going down into a ship (vv. 1-3).

The LORD hurls a great wind on the sea until the ship threatens to break up. The sailors are afraid and each cries to his own god, throwing the cargo overboard, while Jonah lies asleep in the hold. The captain wakes him and tells him to call on his god (vv. 4-6). They cast lots, the lot falls on Jonah, and he tells them he is a Hebrew who fears the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land. The men are exceedingly afraid, for he has told them he is fleeing from God (vv. 7-10).

As the sea grows wilder, Jonah tells them to throw him into it. They row hard to reach land instead, and when they cannot, they call on the LORD not to hold them guilty of innocent blood, and throw Jonah overboard. The sea grows calm, and the men fear the LORD, offer a sacrifice and make vows (vv. 11-16). And the LORD appoints a great fish to swallow Jonah, who is in its belly three days and three nights (v. 17).
1.theology:
God's call comes to his servants on his terms, and includes the people we would rather he left alone (vv. 1-2).

No one can escape God's presence; disobedience is a downward road, and it is never free (v. 3; Ps 139:7-10).

God rules wind, sea, lots and fish, and he pursues his straying servants with providences that feel like disasters and are actually mercies (vv. 4, 7, 17; Prov 16:33).

A believer's sin drags others into the storm, and outsiders often see it more clearly than he does (vv. 5-6, 10).

Correct doctrine held by a disobedient heart is worthless; faith is shown by obedience (vv. 9-10).

One man is thrown into the deep so that others may live — a dim picture of Christ, who suffered the righteous for the unrighteous (vv. 12, 15; John 11:50; 1 Pet 3:18).

God saves whom he will, even pagan sailors through a failing prophet, and the fish itself is rescue, not punishment (vv. 16-17; Matt 12:40-41).
1.examples:
A prophet buying a ticket in the opposite direction.

A believer asleep below deck while unbelievers pray.

A pagan captain telling a prophet to say his prayers.

A creed recited perfectly by a man running away from it.

Sailors digging in their oars to save the man who endangered them.

A sea that falls silent the moment God's word is obeyed.

A fish that looks like the end and turns out to be the rescue.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Jonah prayed to the LORD his God from the belly of the fish,<sup>2</sup>saying, "I called out to the LORD, out of my distress, and he answered me; out of the belly of Sheol I cried, and you heard my voice.<sup>3</sup>For you cast me into the deep, into the heart of the seas, and the flood surrounded me; all your breakers and your waves passed over me.<sup>4</sup>Then I said, 'I am driven away from your sight; yet I shall again look upon your holy temple.'<sup>5</sup>The waters closed in over me to take my life; the deep surrounded me; weeds were wrapped about my head.<sup>6</sup>To the roots of the mountains I went down, to the land whose bars closed upon me forever. Yet you brought up my life from the pit, O LORD my God.<sup>7</sup>When my life was fainting away, I remembered the LORD, and my prayer came to you, into your holy temple.<sup>8</sup>Those who pay regard to vain idols forsake their hope of steadfast love.<sup>9</sup>But I with the voice of thanksgiving will sacrifice to you; what I have vowed I will pay. Salvation belongs to the LORD!"<sup>10</sup>And the LORD spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out upon the dry land.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Out of the Belly of Sheol
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then Jonah prayed to the LORD his God from the belly of the fish (v. 1). He tells how he called out out of my distress, and God answered (v. 2). For you cast me into the deep, with all God's breakers and waves passing over him (v. 3). Driven from God's sight, he still says, yet I shall again look upon your holy temple (v. 4). The waters closed in, weeds wrapped his head, the mountains' roots and the bars of the land shut him in, Yet you brought up my life from the pit (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: From the lowest place a believer can fall, God hears prayer and lifts him out.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jonah prayed to the LORD his God from the belly of the fish, saying, "I called out to the LORD, out of my distress, and he answered me; out of the belly of Sheol I cried, and you heard my voice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jonah prayed to the LORD his God from the belly of the fish,

At last Jonah prays. He would not pray on the ship, even when the captain begged him to (1:6). It sometimes takes the bottom of the sea to open a believer's mouth.

Notice two small phrases. First, the LORD his God. Jonah has run, disobeyed and been thrown overboard, and God is still his God. The relationship held when Jonah did not. Second, from the belly of the fish. There is no place so dark or so strange that prayer cannot reach God from it.

saying, "I called out to the LORD, out of my distress, and he answered me; out of the belly of Sheol I cried, and you heard my voice.

The whole chapter is a prayer, and it is mostly a song of thanks. Jonah looks back on the moment he went under the water and says that he called out and God answered.

Sheol is the Old Testament word for the realm of the dead, the grave. Jonah is saying that he was as good as dead. He had gone as low as a man can go.

Those who know the Psalms will hear them all through this prayer. In my distress I called upon the LORD ... From his temple he heard my voice (Ps 18:6). Jonah is praying in the words of Israel's hymnbook. That is what Scripture is for. When we are too frightened or ashamed to find words of our own, God's own words become our prayer, and a believer who has filled his mind with Scripture in calm days will find it there in the dark.

verseByVerse.quote: For you cast me into the deep, into the heart of the seas, and the flood surrounded me; all your breakers and your waves passed over me. Then I said, 'I am driven away from your sight; yet I shall again look upon your holy temple.' The waters closed in over me to take my life; the deep surrounded me; weeds were wrapped about my head. To the roots of the mountains I went down, to the land whose bars closed upon me forever. Yet you brought up my life from the pit, O LORD my God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you cast me into the deep, into the heart of the seas, and the flood surrounded me; all your breakers and your waves passed over me.

Look carefully at who threw Jonah into the sea. The sailors picked him up and hurled him overboard (1:15), and it was Jonah's own idea. But he prays, you cast me into the deep. He sees God's hand behind the sailors' hands. They are your breakers and your waves. The psalmist had said the same: all your breakers and your waves have gone over me (Ps 42:7).

This is not fatalism, and it does not excuse anyone. It is the comfort of knowing that nothing reaches us except through God's hand. A Christian in a hospital bed or a collapsing business is not in the grip of blind chance.

Then I said, 'I am driven away from your sight; yet I shall again look upon your holy temple.'

Here the prayer turns, on one word: yet. Jonah had tried to flee from the presence of the LORD (1:3); now, sinking, his fear is that he is driven away from your sight. We only discover how much we want God when we think we have lost him.

And then faith speaks: yet I shall again look upon your holy temple. Israelites prayed toward the temple in Jerusalem, the place where God had promised to meet his people and hear them (1 Kgs 8:38-39). Jonah believes he will stand there again. This is faith in its bare form: no evidence, no way out, simply the confidence that God will not abandon him.

The waters closed in over me to take my life; the deep surrounded me; weeds were wrapped about my head.

To the roots of the mountains I went down, to the land whose bars closed upon me forever. Yet you brought up my life from the pit, O LORD my God.

The description is vivid enough to make a reader hold his breath: water closing over his head, weeds tangled around him, sinking past the roots of the mountains. The bars are the gates of the world of the dead, shutting behind him forever. This is where Jonah's journey downward ends, which began when he went down to Joppa (1:3).

Then the second Yet: you brought up my life from the pit. The direction is finally reversed, and God is the one who reverses it. The psalm says it too: O LORD, you have brought up my soul from Sheol (Ps 30:3). A man cannot climb back up from the roots of the mountains. He can only be carried.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–10 — Salvation Belongs to the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When my life was fainting away, I remembered the LORD, and his prayer reached God's holy temple (v. 7). Those who pay regard to vain idols forsake their hope of steadfast love (v. 8). Jonah promises thanksgiving and vows, and cries, Salvation belongs to the LORD! (v. 9). And the LORD spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out upon the dry land (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Salvation is God's to give, not ours to earn or to ration out to the people we approve of.

verseByVerse.quote: When my life was fainting away, I remembered the LORD, and my prayer came to you, into your holy temple. Those who pay regard to vain idols forsake their hope of steadfast love. But I with the voice of thanksgiving will sacrifice to you; what I have vowed I will pay. Salvation belongs to the LORD!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When my life was fainting away, I remembered the LORD, and my prayer came to you, into your holy temple.

I remembered the LORD. Not that he had forgotten God's existence; he had been living as if God did not matter. Remembering, in the Bible, means turning the whole attention back to God and acting on it.

And his prayer travelled. From the bottom of the sea, inside a fish, it came to you, into your holy temple. No distance, no depth and no disgrace can block the prayer of a child of God.

Those who pay regard to vain idols forsake their hope of steadfast love.

An idol is anything we trust to do for us what only God can do, and it is always vain, empty. Those who cling to such things forsake their hope of steadfast love: they walk away from the one love that would never fail them.

Jonah is right, and there is a sting in it that he may not have felt. He had just watched pagan sailors abandon their gods and worship the LORD (1:16), while he himself, who knew better, had run away. The truth we preach has a way of turning around to face us.

But I with the voice of thanksgiving will sacrifice to you; what I have vowed I will pay. Salvation belongs to the LORD!"

The prayer ends with the sentence that holds the whole book together: Salvation belongs to the LORD! It is a line straight out of the Psalms (Ps 3:8). It means that rescue is not something we achieve, arrange or deserve. It is God's, and he gives it as he pleases.

Jonah says these words in the dark, and means them about himself. In chapter 4 he will discover that they are also true about Nineveh, and he will find that much harder. It is easy to celebrate that salvation belongs to the LORD when he gives it to us; it is another thing when he gives it to people we cannot stand.

The New Testament says the same in other words: By grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God (Eph 2:8). And in heaven the same cry goes up from a countless crowd from every nation: Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb! (Rev 7:10).

Two things stand out in this prayer. Jonah gives thanks before he is rescued; he is still inside the fish when he says it. That is real faith, thanking God for a deliverance he cannot yet see. But also, for all its beauty, the prayer never actually confesses the flight, and it never mentions Nineveh. Readers often notice that a man can pray a thoroughly biblical prayer and still be holding on to the very thing God is dealing with. Chapter 4 will show that this is exactly what has happened.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out upon the dry land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the LORD spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out upon the dry land.

God spoke to the fish. He speaks, and the sea creature obeys instantly, which is more than can be said for the prophet. Everything in this book does what God says except the man who knows him best.

And the rescue is not dignified. Jonah is vomited out onto the beach, filthy and half-drowned. God's grace saves us; it does not flatter us. Many a rescued believer has had to begin again in an undignified heap, and it is still grace.

Notice also that he lands on the dry land, the very thing he had confessed God made (1:9), and the place where obedience is possible again. God brings his servant back to the beginning, and in the next chapter the call will come a second time.

Most importantly, Jesus took this chapter and made it a sign of himself: just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth (Matt 12:40). But hear the difference. Jonah prayed from the deep and was heard and lifted out. On the cross, Jesus cried, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Matt 27:46) and was not spared. He went down into death not for his own sin but for ours, and came up on the third day. Because he did, Salvation belongs to the LORD is not merely something we admire; it is something we can have.

2.title: Salvation Belongs to the LORD
2.overview:
From inside the fish Jonah prays to the LORD his God. He tells how he called out of his distress and God answered him, how he cried from the belly of Sheol and was heard (vv. 1-2). God cast him into the deep, and all God's breakers and waves passed over him; driven from God's sight, he still said he would look again on God's holy temple (vv. 3-4). The waters closed over his life, weeds wrapped his head, he sank to the roots of the mountains and the bars of the land closed on him, yet God brought his life up from the pit (vv. 5-6).

As his life was fainting away he remembered the LORD, and his prayer reached God's holy temple (v. 7). Those who cling to vain idols forsake their hope of steadfast love (v. 8). With the voice of thanksgiving he promises to sacrifice and to pay his vows, and cries, "Salvation belongs to the LORD!" (v. 9). Then the LORD speaks to the fish, and it vomits Jonah out on the dry land (v. 10).
2.theology:
God remains the God of his straying servant, and prayer reaches him from any depth (vv. 1-2, 7; Ps 18:6).

Believers may recognise God's hand behind the means that bring them low, without excusing anyone's sin (v. 3; Ps 42:7).

Faith speaks its "yet" when there is no evidence, trusting that God will not abandon his own (v. 4; Ps 31:22).

No one raises himself from the pit; salvation is God's work from first to last (v. 6; Ps 30:3; Eph 2:8-9).

Idols are empty, and those who trust them abandon the only steadfast love there is (v. 8).

Salvation belongs to the LORD, to give as he pleases, which is a comfort when it comes to us and a test when it comes to others (v. 9; Ps 3:8; Rev 7:10).

Jonah's three days in the deep are a sign of Christ, who went down into death for sinners and rose (vv. 1-10; Matt 12:40; Matt 27:46).
2.examples:
A man who would not pray on deck praying inside a fish.

Israel's hymnbook becoming a drowning man's words.

Seaweed wrapped round the head of a sinking prophet.

One word, "yet", turning a prayer around.

Thanksgiving offered before the rescue arrives.

A fish that obeys God instantly, and a prophet who does not.

Grace that saves a man and leaves him in an undignified heap on the beach.
